lessons.title: Choose Appropriate Measures
lessons.objective: I can choose the best measure of center for a data set based on its shape.
lessons.languageObjective: I can explain my choice using the words mean, median, outlier, and skewed.

concept.heading: Should I use the mean or the median?
concept.intro: The mean and the median both describe the center of a data set, but one fits better depending on the shape. When the data has an outlier (a value far from the rest), the median is usually the better choice.
concept.keyIdea: Choosing Appropriate Measures of Center & Spread. 1. Symmetric Data (No Outliers): Use Mean and MAD. 2. Skewed Data (Has Outliers): Use Median and IQR (outliers distort the mean). 3. Compare distributions using both center (typical value) and spread (variability)

worked.title: Watch me
lines: My data, the top scorer's points: 22, 24, 20, 25, 23, 21, 58. I notice 58 is much bigger than the rest, so it is an outlier.
Median: in order they are 20, 21, 22, 23, 24, 25, 58. The middle (4th) value is 23.
The mean (27.6) is higher than 6 of the 7 games because 58 pulled it up. So the median (23) better shows a typical game.
linesEs: Mis datos, los puntos del máximo anotador: 22, 24, 20, 25, 23, 21, 58. Noto que 58 es mucho mayor que el resto, así que es un valor atípico.
Mediana: en orden quedan 20, 21, 22, 23, 24, 25, 58. El valor del medio (el 4.º) es 23.
La media (27.6) es mayor que 6 de los 7 partidos porque 58 la jaló hacia arriba. Así que la mediana (23) muestra mejor un partido típico.

together.title: Let's try together
lines: Data set A: 4, 5, 6, 7, 8. Are there any outliers? If not, which measure should we use, mean or median?
Data set B: 4, 5, 6, 7, 40. Which value is an outlier here?
For data set B, would the outlier pull the mean up or down? So which measure best shows a typical value?
linesEs: Conjunto de datos A: 4, 5, 6, 7, 8. ¿Hay valores atípicos? Si no, ¿qué medida deberíamos usar, la media o la mediana?
Conjunto de datos B: 4, 5, 6, 7, 40. ¿Cuál valor es el atípico aquí?
En el conjunto B, ¿el valor atípico jalaría la media hacia arriba o hacia abajo? Entonces, ¿qué medida muestra mejor un valor típico?

vocabulary.definition: A mean, median, or mode chosen because it describes a data set fairly.
vocabulary.example: Use the median when an outlier would pull the mean too far.

vocabulary.definition: The average. Add all the numbers, then divide by how many there are.
The middle number when you put them in order.
A number that is much bigger or smaller than the rest.
vocabulary.example: Data: 12, 14, 13, 15, 45 → 45 is far from the cluster, so it is an outlier

vocabulary.definition: When most data sits on one side with a tail on the other.
vocabulary.example: Scores: 5, 6, 7, 8, 8, 35 → most scores are low, but 35 creates a tail to the right (skewed right)

vocabulary.definition: How the data looks: where it sits and how spread out it is.
vocabulary.example: Symmetric = even on both sides. Skewed = bunched on one side with a tail

vocabulary.definition: How spread out the numbers are.
Values bunched close together in one part of a display.
vocabulary.example: Values packed near 3 on the dot plot.

vocabulary.definition: A space on a display where no data values fall.
vocabulary.example: Nothing between 11 and 32 on the number line.

title: The Outlier Investigation
mission: A dramatic number has changed a report. Investigate which measures still describe a typical observation honestly.
investigate: Compare the mean and median. Which one is closer to most values?

Explain when keeping an unusual value is important even if it changes the summary.
create: Write two accurate reports about the same data: one using mean and MAD, the other median and IQR. Recommend the more useful report and justify your choice.

support.prompt: A gymnast's scores are: 8.5, 8.8, 8.7, 8.6, 8.9. There are no outliers. Which measure best represents a typical score?
choices: Neither — the data is too small
support.explanation: The data is symmetric with no outliers, so the mean (8.7) best represents the typical score.
feedback: The median ignores how far apart the values are. Check whether this data has any outlier that would make leaving values out worthwhile.
Five values is plenty for a measure of center. A small set is only a problem when it contains extreme values.
Both measures actually work reasonably well here, since the scores are clustered close together. Decide which one uses the data most fully when there are no outliers.
hints: Look at the scores: 8.5 up to 8.9 — all five are bunched tightly together with no unusual value.
Rule of thumb: with no outliers and balanced data, one measure uses every value fairly. With outliers, the middle value is safer. Which case is this?
First step: check for an outlier — is any score far from the others? All five sit within 0.4 points, so apply the no-outlier rule.

support.prompt: A runner's mile times are: 7:10, 7:15, 7:12, 7:20, 12:00. The 12:00 was due to a cramp. Which measure best represents a typical mile?
choices: Mean — it uses all the data
Median — the outlier 12:00 pulls the mean too high
Mode — it shows the most common time
support.explanation: The 12:00 is an outlier that pulls the mean up. The median (7:15) better represents the runner's typical time.
feedback: Mean uses all data—but the outlier pulls it too high.
Mode shows most common—but doesn't handle the outlier well.
Both measures exist, but which resists the 12:00 outlier?
hints: Four times are near 7 minutes; one is 12:00 from a cramp. That 12:00 is an outlier, not a typical mile.
Ask: which measure gets dragged toward an extreme value, and which one just takes the middle of the ordered list?
First step: order the times and notice where 12:00 sits — far beyond the rest. Then choose the measure that isn't pulled by that extreme time.

support.prompt: Data set: 5, 6, 7, 7, 8, 50. The mean is about 13.8 and the median is 7. Which better represents the typical value?
choices: Median (7) — the outlier 50 inflates the mean
support.explanation: The mean (13.8) is higher than 5 of the 6 values because the outlier 50 pulls it up. The median (7) better represents a typical value.
feedback: Mean uses all data—but 50 pulls it way above 5 of the 6 values.
Both exist, but which is closer to most of the data points?
One works well for typical value—use the one that resists 50.
hints: Five of the six values are between 5 and 8 — then there's 50. Notice where the mean (13.8) lands compared to those five.
Test for 'typical': count how many actual data values sit near 13.8, then how many sit near 7. A good measure stays close to most of the data.
First step: compare 13.8 to the list — it's bigger than 5, 6, 7, 7, AND 8. Ask what pulled it up there, and whether the median has that problem.

support.prompt: Spot the Mistake — Forgetting to Order the Data
steps: Data: A swimmer's lap counts: 9, 12, 8, 11, 10 (no outliers).
Find the median: The student keeps the numbers as written (9, 12, 8, 11, 10) and picks the middle one: median = 8.
Choose a measure: The student reports the median (8) as the typical lap count.
support.explanation: You must put the data in order before finding the median. In order: 8, 9, 10, 11, 12. The middle value is 10, so the median is 10 (not 8). Since there are no outliers, the mean (10) and median (10) agree, and either is a fine measure of a typical lap.
hints: The median is the MIDDLE value only after the numbers are sorted from least to greatest.
Sort the data first: 8, 9, 10, 11, 12. Now which value sits in the middle?

core.prompt: A baseball player's batting averages over 6 seasons are: .280, .295, .290, .285, .300, .110. The .110 was an injury-shortened season. Which measure better represents the player's typical batting average?
choices: Median, because the .110 outlier pulls the mean down
Mean, because it uses all the data
Mean, because .110 is a real season
core.explanation: The .110 is an outlier that pulls the mean down to .260. The median (.2875) better represents typical performance because it isn't affected by the extreme value.
feedback: Mean uses all data—but the .110 outlier pulls it down.
Even though .110 is real, which measure shows typical performance better?
Both measures exist, but which resists the .110 outlier?
hints: Five seasons sit between .280 and .300; the .110 season is far below them — a low outlier.
A low outlier drags one measure DOWN below the player's usual level. Think about which measure uses only the middle of the ordered list.
First step: order the six averages and find the two middle ones. Notice that .110 sits at the far end and never touches that middle.

core.prompt: Spot the Mistake — Choosing the Mean Despite an Outlier
steps: Data: A receiver's catches per game: 12, 14, 13, 15, 11, 60 (the 60 was a record-setting playoff game).
Find the mean: Sum = 125, Count = 6, Mean = 125 ÷ 6 ≈ 20.8.
Choose a measure: The student reports the mean (≈ 20.8) as the typical number of catches because it uses every game.
core.explanation: The student should report the median (13.5), not the mean. The 60-catch game is an outlier that pulls the mean up to about 20.8 — higher than 5 of the 6 games. The median (13.5) is resistant to that outlier and better represents a typical game.
hints: Compare the mean (≈ 20.8) to the actual games. Is it close to a typical value, or higher than almost all of them?
When one value (60) is far from the rest, it pulls the mean. The median (13.5) stays near the cluster, so it is the better choice.

stretch.prompt: A local newspaper reports that the average home price in a neighborhood is $450,000. The actual prices are: $180K, $200K, $190K, $210K, $195K, $1,725K. Is the reporter's claim misleading? Calculate the mean and median and explain which better represents a 'typical' home price.
stretch.frame: Mean = ___. Median = ___. The reporter's claim is ___ because the outlier ($1,725K) pulls the mean ___. The ___ (about $___) better represents a typical home price because ___.
stretch.explanation: The six prices add to $2,700K, so the mean is 2,700 ÷ 6 = $450K, matching the reporter — but the median is the average of the middle two prices, $195K and $200K, which is $197.5K. Five of the six homes cost between $180K and $210K, so the $1,725K home is an outlier pulling the mean far above what most homes cost. The claim is misleading, and the median better represents a typical price.
hints: Five homes cost about $180K–$210K; one costs $1,725K. Check the reporter's $450,000 'average' against those five real prices.
Plan: (1) mean = sum of all six prices ÷ 6, (2) median = average of the 3rd and 4th ordered prices, (3) compare each to what most homes cost.
Step 1: add 180 + 200 + 190 + 210 + 195 + 1725 (in thousands) and divide by 6. Then order the six prices and average the middle two.
